newsitem.title: USA: Potential Oklahoma bomb trial jurors meet judge.
newsitem.headline: Potential Oklahoma bomb trial jurors meet judge.

text.p: Prospective jurors in the Oklahoma City bombing trial met the judge and attorneys on Wednesday amid tight security at a fairground outside Denver.

Potential jurors were asked to fill out questionnaires to be used to help pick a jury for the trial of suspect Timothy McVeigh, scheduled to start March 31. Some 1,000 notices were sent out to residents of Denver and 22 surrounding counties last month in hopes of finding 12 jurors and six alternates.

A court official refused to disclose details of the meeting. "The judge has issued an order that there be no discussion whatsoever of any of the jury selection process by any of the participants, staff, attorneys or any of the participants," James Manspeaker, spokesman for U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch, told reporters.

Matsch has said the gathering was not considered a pre-trial hearing and was therefore closed to the public and the press. The questionnaire was not made public. About 500 prospective jurors arrived at the Jefferson County Fairgrounds, about 12 miles from the federal courthouse in downtown Denver, behind tight security.

"We just thought this would be enough," Manspeaker said earlier, referring to the number of people called in. The fairground was chosen because its auditorium had a larger capacity than any courtroom, he said.

McVeigh and co-defendant Terry Nichols are charged in the April 19, 1995, bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building that killed 168 people. They will be tried separately and no date has been set for Nichols' trial.
Families of several bombing victims on Wednesday said they planned to sue the federal government for failing to warn of a possible terrorist attack on the building two years ago.

The families of at least 44 victims alleged the government knew or should have known that federal buildings could be targeted by groups for violent acts on April 19, the anniversary of a government raid on the Branch Davidian religious compound in Waco, Texas.

Reporters and photographers were kept about 200 yards from the auditorium where the potential jurors assembled Wednesday. Matsch has said special arrangements were made to protect the privacy of the jury, and the names of those who received notices have not been released.

Also Wednesday, an Oklahoma City newspaper said a Texas private investigator who worked with McVeigh's defence team had denied faking a confession by McVeigh. The Dallas Morning News last month said it had obtained documents containing a confession from McVeigh, but his defence lawyers said the confession was a ruse to try to prompt a witness to speak with the defence.

The Daily Oklahoman said defence investigator Richard Reyna would not say whether McVeigh confessed during interviews but quoted him as saying: "I would not go and falsify anything. It's just not going to happen with me."
The defence never identified the investigator involved in the ruse but a reporter at an Oklahoma newspaper said he was shown the purported confession by Reyna and knew it was a fake.
